messages.content: Who are the famous dancers of the 19th Century?

function.name: get_museum_artists

message.content:
**Famous 19th‑century dancers (ballet and other classical styles)**  

| Dancer | Nationality | Notable achievements / roles |
|--------|-------------|------------------------------|
| **Marie Taglioni** (1815–1897) | Swiss | Pioneered “en pointe” technique; star of *La Sylphide* and *Giselle*. Her ethereal style defined Romantic ballet. |
| **Fanny Elssler** (1800–1871) | Austrian | Virtuosic virtuosity and dramatic expressiveness; famed for *La Sylphide*, *Giselle*, and *Coppélia*. |
| **Carlotta Grisi** (1819–1893) | Italian | Star of *La Sylphide* (with Taglioni) and *Giselle*; known for lyrical phrasing and technical precision. |
| **Jules Perrot** (1793–1869) | French | Dancer‑choreographer; created *La Sylphide* (first version) and *Coppélia*. Influenced the Romantic ballet vocabulary. |
| **August Bournonville** (1805–1879) | Danish | Dancer‑choreographer; developed the distinct Bournonville style (lightness, quick footwork) and choreographed *La Sylphide* (Bournonville version). |
| **Marius Petipa** (born 1848) | Russian | Though best known as a choreographer, he began as a dancer in the Imperial Ballet. His later work (late 19th c.) shaped the classical repertoire. |
| **Carlo Blasis** (1815–1882) | Italian | Dancer‑teacher; authored *L’arte della danza* (1840), a foundational text on ballet technique. |
| **Anna Pavlova** (1881–1931) | Russian | Though her career peaked in the early 20th c., she was trained in the 19th‑century tradition and helped popularize the solo ballerina. |
| **John L. (John L. —)** | — | *[Optional: include other notable dancers such as John L. (if known)]* |

These performers were central to the development of Romantic ballet and set the stage for the modern classical ballet tradition. Their virtuosity, expressive artistry, and innovations in technique made them household names in Europe and beyond during the 19th century.
